Liverpool are beginning to see the very best of Florian Wirtz if recent form is anything to go by

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.

Supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans. His debut campaign proved an awkward adaptation to English football, one in which the German seemed caught between systems, clearly in transition.

Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.

Wirtz produced a standout display in Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing of Manchester United, where he scored an improvised goal to extend the Reds' lead and created 10 chances - albeit against 10 men - before finding the net again in Wednesday night’s 3-0 Champions League triumph over Club Brugge.

The underlying numbers from Gradient Sports prove this is no fleeting purple patch, either, especially after three goals in two games over the November international break.

According to Gradient Sports’ data, Wirtz’s overall player grade dipped sharply from a league-leading 91.0 in his final Bundesliga season with Leverkusen in 2024/25 to 73.1 during his debut 2025/26 Premier League campaign.

While his overall 2026/27 Premier League grade sits at 73.9, his attacking execution indicates a resurgence back toward his Leverkusen peak.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In the Premier League this season, Wirtz has had a 48 per cent increase in chances created - jumping from 1.99 to 2.94 per 90 minutes - ranking first among all Premier League wingers and attacking midfielders.

Even more telling is his cutting edge in the final third: Wirtz's passes directly leading to a half-chance have increased by 84 per cent, from 0.31 to 0.57 per 90.

His end product in front of goal tells a similar story. Gradient data notes that Wirtz’s positively graded shots have risen from 0.24 to 0.38 per 90 - closing in on the 0.45 he posted in 2024/25. Similarly, his 1.61 shots in the box per 90 actually surpasses his final Leverkusen tally of 1.60.

So, what has initiated the turnaround? New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola deserves credit for tweaking Wirtz's role and adjusting the team's tempo, but Anfield may also owe a debt of gratitude to Jurgen Klopp.

Since taking charge of the German national team, Klopp has turned Wirtz into his talisman; he has four goals in his last four international appearances. And it's that confidence which has bled into his club form, aided by private counsel from the former Reds manager. Wirtz revealed recently that he regularly speaks with Klopp about life at Anfield, taking on board "small, private things" from a man who knows exactly how to win over the Kop.

Armed with Klopp’s guidance and backed by the evidence of improved creative metrics in the Premier League, Liverpool’s £116m man is finally beginning to look worthy of his price tag.

#859. Levski Sofia fans hospitalised after violent clashes with Marseille supporters

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Bulgarian Football Union has referred the incident to Uefa

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Marseille head coach Bruno Genesio said “we are living through violent times” after five Levski Sofia fans were hospitalised following violent clashes before their Europa League encounter with the French side.

Groups of supporters threw projectiles and flares and French outlet L’Equipe reported that there were Nazi salutes observed in the away section.

Ten minutes before kick-off at the Stade Velodrome a group of Marseille fans broke through into the away stand, which housed around 500 fans.

In the ensuing clashes five people, all Bulgarian, were injured and taken to hospital “with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder”, according to the Marseille police prefecture, while six others were treated on-site for more superficial injuries.

The police force said there was “no information at this stage regarding any arrests”.

Security were able to restore order and the game kicked off on time, although there were further incidents later on, particularly at half-time.

Genesio said: “We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable.” Julio Velazquez, head coach of the Bulgarian domestic champions, said: “It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football.”

The Bulgarian Football Union condemned the violence and said it had referred the incident to UEFA, calling for the harshest possible sanctions. It also demanded full cooperation and transparency from French authorities in investigating the attacks and identifying those responsible.

Levski said the club's priority is the safety and well-being of its fans. A statement read: “What happened tonight is particularly alarming given the extraordinary security measures put in place by the French authorities, as well as the restrictions imposed on our travelling supporters—restrictions that the club had already formally contested with UEFA.

“Despite the risks identified by the club prior to the match, the measures taken failed to provide adequate protection for our fans. This is completely unacceptable.”

Marseille also condemned the violence and said it is conducting “a thorough analysis of the circumstances in which these incidents took place.”

Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova called for those responsible to be held accountable and Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he had spoken to French president Emmanuel Macron about the violence at a European summit in Brussels.

A spokesperson for Macron’s office said: “He condemned in the strongest possible terms these acts of violence targeting Bulgarian supporters, which have no place in sport or in public spaces, and assured the Prime Minister that these acts would not go unpunished.”

Marseille won the game 1-0, with Amine Gouiri scoring a 28th-minute penalty.

England and Arsenal striker Alessia Russo speaks about football memories and handling pressure in front of goal as she partners with Lucozade

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alessia Russo has two European Championships and a Champions League to her name and has established herself as one of England’s most prolific strikers.

In another impressive year for the 27-year-old, she became the highest-scoring English player in UEFA Women's Champions League history with a recent hat-trick against Benfica, was named England Women's Player of the Year and earned a place in the FIFPRO Women's World 11.

Speaking to former Three Lions striker Ian Wright at the launch of her new long-term partnership with Lucozade, the England and Arsenal forward discussed how she fell in love with football and the mentality behind her performances.

Russo grew up in Maidstone, Kent and football always featured in her life.

“Football has always been a massive part of my life,” she said. “Growing up, my dad would take me to watch women’s games at Charlton, and I remember looking up to those players and dreaming of doing the same one day.

“To see how far the game has come is incredible. Women’s football is now about so much more than what happens on the pitch. It’s influencing fashion, culture and bringing communities together in ways I could never have imagined growing up.

“To be part of that journey is really special.”

Now one of the leading strikers in world football, Russo believes her calm approach is one of her biggest strengths when it comes to finding the back of the net.

"I've always been really laid back. I'm always wanting to win. Just because I'm not angry or shouting or screaming, doesn't mean I don't want to win and I don't want to score," she said.

"I think that calmness is something that I try and bring to the game. And I think as a striker, you have to be calm in and around the box. When things aren't going your way, I just kind of strip it back. I like to train hard and then whatever happens in the game happens.

"You can't control a whole lot as a No.9. You're quite reliant on other players. But what you can control is the moments that you do get."

The partnership will see Russo work with Lucozade Sport to better understand her individual hydration and fuelling requirements, with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil on the horizon.

She will also help inform future product innovation as the brand continues its longstanding support of the Lionesses, dating back to 2006.

#857. Soldier Reeves emerges as future star with Long Distance Hurdle win

Soldier Reeves banished doubts about his staying ability with a magnificent display in the Coral Long Distance Hurdle. In the feature race, Dan Skelton's charge proved too good for previous winners Impose Toi and Strong Leader - who was gallant in second.

Soldier Reeves emerged as the new kid on the block in the staying division with an impressive comeback victory in the Coral Long Distance Hurdle at Newbury.

Dan Skelton's five-year-old mixed it with the best around in novice hurdles last season, most notably finishing fourth behind King Rasko Grey when upped in trip for the Turners Novices' Hurdle at the Cheltenham Festival before finding only high-class stablemate Bossman Jack too strong at Aintree.

He faced another step into the unknown on his reappearance, taking on more hardened stayers on his first start over three miles under rules, but travelled powerfully throughout in the hands of Harry Skelton and was right on the heels of the redoubtable Strong Leader on the approach to the final flight.

The latter did his best to regain his crown, having emerged victorious two years ago and finished a close second to Impose Toi last term, but Soldier Reeves (3-1) was the stronger at the finish and passed the post with three and a quarter lengths in hand.

Skelton will now point his emerging stayer to Ascot's Long Walk Hurdle just before Christmas.

He said: "I was very impressed with him and I wasn't surprised he won, but I was surprised he could do it first time out.

"He still didn't relax all that well, but he relaxed well enough for Harry to be able to get him switched off and he came home strongly.

"I didn't go to three miles in the spring and this makes me glad I didn't. We may have left a big race behind not going three miles at Aintree, but I just knew if I did that when he was just a five-year-old I might have been asking too much. I trusted him today and he delivered."

He went on: "He was under the radar, but that's because he wasn't quite behaving well enough to win one of those last year.

"I put that down to the fact he was very raw at four and five. We only went hurdling last year because I was so annoyed with him for pulling so hard in a bumper at Newton Abbot that I sent him hurdling to try to slow him down with a few jumps in front of him.

"He has just improved and improved and improved and he has a brilliant engine. He had some good rivals around him at the last and I was very impressed he could come out on top as I thought it was a very competitive renewal.

"I have a lot of respect for the horses he has beaten there and now he will have to try to back it up. The one thing about this horse though is he has a fantastic attitude and we'll go now to the Long Walk."

Race regular Strong Leader could renew rivalry at Ascot, although Olly Murphy will also consider a trip to Ireland.

Murphy said: "He ran well but just bumped into a younger, better horse on the day. We have no excuse whatsoever and although people love to knock this horse and he's not always great at Cheltenham, nine times out of 10 he turns up and runs a great race.

"He always jumps the last looking like the winner, but today he has bumped into a better one and we'll dust ourselves down and go again.

"Whether we go Ascot at Christmas or Ireland, I'm not sure, but there is still life in him yet. He loves a left-handed flat track and yes he ran very well in a Long Walk last year, but Ireland is certainly something we'll have a good look at.

"We'll see how he comes out of today and he's run a cracker and I'm really proud of him. He deserves to win a big one again, but it's life and sometimes you bump into a nice young horse who is just too good on the day."

Taurus Bay followed in the hoofprints of illustrious stablemate The Jukebox Man by winning the Coral John Francome Novices' Chase.

It is two years since Harry Redknapp's subsequent King George hero made a winning debut over fences in this Grade Two contest and in his younger stablemate the popular owner, trainer Ben Pauling and jockey Ben Jones appear to have unearthed another potential star.

Taurus Bay lined up having already won over the larger obstacles in the Rising Stars Novices' Chase at Aintree three weeks ago, a victory which meant the 11-8 favourite had to concede 3lb to each of his four rivals in his bid for back-to-back Group Two wins.

Harry Skelton ensured the race was a stern test of stamina and jumping aboard the front-running Royal Infantry, but Jones steadily nursed Taurus Bay into contention and he toughed it out on the run-in to prevail by half a length.

Pauling said: "It's lovely to work with horses who try as hard as that when they need to. He didn't have the run of the race and was in a tight pocket and Ben was patient when he needed to be today, which was great.

"We all know the Skelton team are going to be very hard to pass and are never here to make up the numbers, but I was always confident jumping two out and after the last he was going to tough it out.

"Ben would have liked him to have travelled a little bit better early doors, but that might have been because the ground was a little lively for him. I would love to get some soft ground for this horse soon because that's when we'll see him at his best.

"We definitely won't be going up in trip and I would come back in trip before I go up. I even think two miles on soft ground could be where he's at his best.

"There were no punches held there and the very good two-milers do stay really well as well. As for the future I would love to keep him at two or two and a half and he could be an Arkle horse - it's an option.

"The obvious place would be (to target) the Manifesto and then you could Wayward Lad (Kempton), Scilly Isles (Sandown) and then Aintree. But it's just lovely to see a horse win two Grade Twos in his first two outings over fences and in doing so he has hardly made a mistake."

Koala Rose looked every inch a filly bound for the big spring festivals judged on an impressive second success over obstacles.

A 77-rated performer on the Flat, having been placed on each of her five starts for Ralph Beckett without quite managing to get her head in front, the daughter of Australia won by 62 lengths on her jumping bow at Hereford, earning her a step up to Listed level in the Coral "Daily Rewards Shaker" Fillies' Juvenile Hurdle.

Supporters of Dan Skelton's exciting recruit will have had few concerns, with the 8-13 favourite jumping nimbly in front throughout in the hands of Harry Skelton before powering 16 lengths clear of another previous winner in Echo Valley on the run-in.

Skelton said: "I thought she was very good and I was delighted to see her win as well as that.

"I think there was a bit of market negativity around some of the others, so you might have to take the form with a pinch of salt. Hereford taught us only that she loves to jump, which we already knew from home, but she was very nimble around Hereford and today she's answered another question.

"There's harder questions to come, but I was really impressed with her attitude and hopefully she is progressive as well and there's more lurking under there.

"Hereford was quick ground, but there on slightly softer ground you could see she was barely getting her toe off the ground and it does play on my mind a little bit. Maybe we shouldn't ask her difficult questions too soon on soft ground and wait for some nicer conditions that allow her to show us what she can do.

"There's a Listed juvenile fillies' race at Doncaster at the end of January and that could be most appropriate. There's sure to be other races open to her as well, but she's a pretty effective three-year-old filly and not many have the substance and aggression in their jumping like she does and it really helps."

#856. Syrian referee refutes ‘drunk’ accusations as ‘insult and defamation’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was replaced at half-time of the AFC Champions League Two match between Gol Gohar and Al Jazira

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A referee has hit back at claims he was “drunk” while officiating an AFC Champions League Two match.

Footage has been widely shared on social media of Syrian referee Hanna Hattab looking visibly disoriented during a match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

One particular incident raised eyebrows when Hattab showed a yellow card to Al Jazira’s goalkeeper for a foul that happened close to the halfway line, 40 yards away from him.

Hattab was then replaced at half-time with the fourth official taking over for the remainder of the game, which Al Jazira won 1-0.

Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following erratic decision-making as similar accusations flooded in online.

But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has refuted the allegations as “insult and defamation”, threatening legal action.

“I also confirm my full right to take all legal and judicial measures against anyone who published or made a statement or contributed to the insult and defamation of me, regardless of their position or status, whether they are an individual, an institution, or a sports entity.”

He also said he would issue a further statement following contact with the Syrian Arab Football Federation (SFA) which will “clarify all the details and facts related to what happened ... with full transparency and clarity.”

Omani journalist Issa Said, who covers Asian football, has since claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

The SFA have also put out a statement standing in support of Hattab, while stating it has requested his medical report from the match.

“The Main Referees Committee of the Syrian Arab Football Federation confirms that it stands in full support of international referee Mr Hana Khattab regarding the incident he was subjected to, following reassurance about his health,” it said.

“This comes after the committee was reassured of his well-being, following a number of discussions on social media concerning the incident. The committee emphasises its full support for him and its commitment to following up on the matter in all its details and developments.

“In this regard, the committee has requested that the Syrian Football Referees Committee provide the medical report relating to the referee, the match observers' report and the referee assessor's report. This is in order to establish the circumstances of the incident accurately and comprehensively and to complete the necessary procedures in this matter.

“The committee also confirms that it will provide the relevant authorities and the public with the findings as soon as the requested reports are received, in order to ensure accuracy and to obtain information from official sources.”

#854. Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

#853. An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.

#852. Europa League match suspended after police clashes over Palestine banner

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute and restarted 30 minutes later

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Europa League game between Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for around 30 minutes on Thursday when police clashed with fans of the Turkish club after they displayed a banner in support of Palestine.

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute but restarted after the interruption.

Turkey’s Haberturk broadcaster said Georgian police used pepper spray against the Besiktas fans, who also unfurled a Palestinian flag, prompting referee referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

In a statement, Besiktas accused the Georgian security forces of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

Georgian police entered the stands and ⁠used pepper spray on Besiktas fans, Turkish outlet NTV reported.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the club said. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”

The report added that Turkish fans chanted “Down with Israel” and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters before play restarted to calm the situation.

The Turkish Football Federation condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters on X, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination. It said it would press for an investigation.

The TFF’s statement read: “We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, conduct and interference directed at Beşiktaş supporters, both inside and outside the stadium, before and during our club’s Uefa Europa League match against Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia.

“No practice that disregards the universal values of sport, human dignity, mutual respect and the principles of fair play, or that involves discrimination, exclusion or security failures, can be tolerated.

“Nor can there be any question of remaining silent in the face of such conduct, which endangers our supporters’ safety and targets their fundamental rights and freedoms.

“As the Turkish Football Federation, we declare unequivocally that we will follow this matter to its conclusion to ensure that the events are fully investigated, those responsible are identified and the necessary sanctions are imposed without delay.

“There must be no tolerance for covering up these events, allowing those responsible to evade accountability or permitting similar violations to recur.

“We emphasize that we stand firmly with our club, Besiktas, and our supporters, who faced a series of problems, particularly serious security failures, and extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our supporters subjected to interference and mistreatment.

“Let no one forget that we will not remain silent in the face of disrespect, discrimination and security violations directed at representatives and supporters of Turkish football.

“We will act decisively on national and international platforms to ensure that all necessary steps are taken, particularly with Uefa, and that those responsible are held accountable.”

Turkish clubs echoed the sentiments of the TFF, with Besiktas’ rivals Fenerbahce, Galatasaray and Trabzonspor all among those to stand with the club.

“We do not accept Turkish clubs being denied the right to play their home matches in their own country, in front of their own fans, when facing clubs from the occupying state of Israel,” Trabzonspor wrote in a statement.

“We do not consider Uefa’s double standards on this issue acceptable. We also strongly condemn the disproportionate intervention by security forces against Besiktas fans in Georgia this evening.”

The ⁠officiating team and the Besiktas players ‌left ​the pitch before ‌the game restarted.

Earlier, the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva and Israel FA had not commented on the incident at the time of publishing.

Spurs are getting things moving in the right direction under Roberto De Zerbi - but there's a missing piece to the puzzle

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tottenham Hotspur’s resurgence under Roberto De Zerbi has breathed fresh life into the club after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes.

There is one clear deficiency in their current make-up that threatens to limit what they can achieve in 2026/27, though - they can't finish.

Despite sitting comfortably in the top half after 12 games, Spurs’ underlying attacking numbers tell the story of a side creating plenty and squandering too much of it.

Tottenham have rattled off 170 shots in the Premier League this season - the fifth-highest tally in the division - while only Liverpool and Manchester City have registered more efforts from inside the penalty area than Spurs’ 109.

But, when it comes to actually hitting the target, De Zerbi’s side slump to 14th across the top flight.

There's also an issue with their ball-striking. According to Gradient Sports’ analysts, just six of Spurs’ 170 league attempts have been graded as ‘unsaveable’ - a figure bettered by every team in the Premier League bar Everton (5).

For context, high-flying Brighton have racked up 20 unsaveable efforts, while Erling Haaland has managed seven on his own. At 3.5 per cent, Tottenham boast the lowest proportion of unsaveable shots in the entire division.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

A glance at De Zerbi’s attacking options explains why to some extent. Richarlison has been frozen out entirely and is angling for a January move, Dominic Solanke has managed just two league goals, and big-money summer arrival Omar Marmoush is yet to hit the ground running in north London.

Centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is the team's joint-top Premier League goalscorer with two goals after 12 matches: Spurs need a centre-forward in January.

Enter Real Sociedad’s 22-year-old Icelandic international Orri Oskarsson.

Oskarsson is by no means LaLiga’s most prolific frontman, having netted four times in the Spanish top flight this term but his underlying metrics point towards a striker ready to thrive in a possession-heavy, attack-minded system.

Unlike De Zerbi’s Spurs, Real Sociedad do not dominate the ball as often, leaving their striker without service for large periods of matches. Oskarsson, though, is making every second count when his team are in possession, averaging a goal every 64 minutes that La Real actually have the ball this season.

In total, he has scored nine times across his last 13 appearances for club and country.

What makes Oskarsson particularly suited to Tottenham is how intelligently he moves to receive the ball. Gradient Sports’ data shows the Icelandic forward receives line-breaking passes 45 per cent of the time, placing him among LaLiga’s best at peeling off defenders and making himself available to creative midfielders.

That off-the-ball awareness is reinforced by the fact he has received the ball in a clear shooting position 10 times in the league this season - a tally bettered only by Barcelona’s Raphinha (13) and Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe (11).

Once the ball arrives at his feet, Oskarsson has the penalty-box nous Tottenham lack. Ninety-two per cent of his LaLiga shots this season have been taken from inside the box, which aligns nicely with the 109 close-range openings Spurs have already generated this term. Even more impressive, out of the 25 shots he has taken in LaLiga, five have been graded as unsaveable by Gradient's analysts - just one fewer than Tottenham’s entire squad combined.

Gradient have also flagged just one occasion all season where Oskarsson opted to shoot when passing to a better-placed teammate was the superior option, highlighting good judgement under pressure and decision-making that is rare for a 22-year-old.

Meanwhile, his Expected Goals (xG) ranks sixth-highest in LaLiga - a decent return given Real Sociedad’s modest share of possession and chance creation.

And best of all, a winter deal is entirely plausible. For a Tottenham side creating plenty of penalty-box opportunities but with nobody reliable to tuck them away, Oskarsson could be one of the more shrewd January investments the market has to offer.

#850. Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."

France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

The court heard the international footballer was filmed by a cyclist while he was stationary in traffic

Newcastle United star Sven Botman has been banned from driving after he was caught using his mobile phone at the wheel.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed that Botman, 26, pleaded guilty at Newcastle Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

The Dutch international defender was given six penalty points and disqualified from driving for six months, as these were added to points he had already accrued.

The MoJ said Botman was fined £900 and ordered to pay £400 costs and a £360 surcharge.

Court documents show that Botman was in a Land Rover on the A189 Haddricks Mill Road, in Newcastle, on 17 September when he was spotted using his phone.

According to The Sun, the court heard he was filmed by a cyclist while he was stationary in traffic.

The Dutch centre-half was signed by Newcastle in a £32 million deal from French club Lille during the summer of 2022.

Since signing for the Magpies, Botman has made 124 appearances and was part of the squad that won the League Cup in 2025, their first major trophy in decades.

Panini have launched their latest Barclays Women's Super League sticker collection, featuring teams from WSL and WSL 2 for a second year running.

This is only the fourth edition of the book for the top women’s league in this country, and Rachel Daly believes the culture of sticker collecting can play its part in growing the women’s game.

As the latest collection was launched in London this week, the ex-Lioness spoke to FourFourTwo about the rise of the women's game.

Speaking at the launch, Daly reflected on her own childhood memories of collecting Panini stickers.

"For me, it goes back to my childhood,” Daly told FourFourTwo. “I collected them with my brother. We used to, every Saturday morning, go and get the stickers.

"You'd get your piles and you'd trade them and swap them at school. Just that whole feeling of sitting down and putting stickers in.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I'm a Leeds fan, so I always wanted to get the whole Leeds team immediately when I was younger.

"I would literally swap any of my stickers, even if I'd already got the Leeds player, just to have more.”

While Daly grew up collecting men’s players, this WSL collection offers an opportunity to introduce more fans to the women's game, something Daly believes is particularly important as the league continues to grow.

The latest album has 545 stickers across all 26 WSL and WSL2 clubs, giving fans access to collect stickers of their favourite players from across the top two tiers of English women’s football.

"The visibility of the game is massive," she added.

"For the fact that it's WSL 1 and 2, I think it's equally as important. Those players in the WSL 2 deserve the same recognition as us.

"Being able to see kids being exposed to seeing the women's game as well, it's exciting."

Daly was speaking at the launch of the Panini Barclays Women's Super League Official Sticker Collection 2027 in London. The collection is available now at retailers nationwide and online via Panini.co.uk.

Messi played his last game for Argentina in October

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Lionel Messi will play his first match in Argentina since his international retirement when he takes part in Carlos Tevez’s testimonial in December.

Messi called time on his 21-year career with La Albiceleste in October, scoring his 126th and final Argentina goal in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin.

It was an emotional send-off for a player that is deified in his homeland, but Argentinians haven’t had to wait long for Messi to come back, with the 39-year-old confirming his next footballing commitment in the country.

The Inter Miami superstar will feature in the testimonial match of his former international team-mate Tevez, which is being held at Boca Juniors’ iconic stadium La Bombonera.

Tevez saw out his career at boyhood club Boca Juniors in 2022, bringing down the curtain on a career that included spells at Manchester City, Manchester United and Juventus.

Tevez made 76 caps and scored 13 times for Argentina, winning an Olympic gold medal with his country at the 2004 Games.

Nicknamed “Apache”, 42-year-old Tevez said last year he wanted Messi and former United team-mate Cristiano Ronaldo to play on opposing teams in his testimonial.

And while Ronaldo will not be involved barring a dramatic late addition, Messi will turn out for a man he shared the international stage with for a decade.

"It will be a ⁠true honour to welcome the best player in the world to Apache’s last dance," organisers posted on Instagram on Thursday.

Other stars involved in Tevez’s testimonial includes ex-United team-mate Rio Ferdinand, former City strike-partner Sergio Aguero and goalkeeper Gianluigi Buffon, who was Tevez’s captain at Juventus.

Victor Munoz is in a race against time to be fit for Sunday’s Merseyside derby as Liverpool could be without three midfielders or wingers.

Cody Gakpo will definitely miss the trip to Everton while Ryan Gravenberch is unlikely to be available.

Summer signing Munoz went off in Wednesday’s 3-0 win over Club Brugge with a knee problem he sustained in a collision and while Liverpool are confident there is no major problem, they are waiting to see if he can play at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

“With Victor, I think the good news is after assessing him, there is no [structural damage] in the knee but he has a big knock,” said head coach Andoni Iraola. “He hasn’t trained [on Friday] but he wants to try tomorrow so we will see. I cannot tell you right now.

Gakpo was injured on international duty with the Netherlands and has missed Liverpool’s last two games and Iraola suggested he could be a doubt for next Saturday’s game against Chelsea.

“Cody is definitely not [in contention for Everton],” Iraola added. “He has a muscle injury so we have to wait a little bit until the process goes on and it heals.

“This kind of injury is normally about two or three weeks. He did it in the last game against Germany so normally so normally it is this timeline. Normally, I don’t like to say timelines with injury because every injury is different and some of them go quicker than others. Normally, this isn’t a big injury but there is something there and you have to give it the time to heal.”

Midfielder Gravenberch has an issue with his heel and Iraola does not expect him to face Everton.

“I think it is going to be difficult, I cannot say no but this kind of injuries but he has the pain and doesn’t go,” he added.

The parallels between the Hammers and the Foxes are impossible to ignore as Scott Parker’s team slide down the Championship table

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Relegation can be the best thing that can happen to a club.

It offers the chance to reset, for fans to enjoy going to games again and for the team to come back stronger, with a clearer plan and greater purpose.

Sometimes, though, relegation is just the start. If it is not taken seriously, relegation might not be rock-bottom, but a trapdoor that sends a club spiralling to new lows.

Leicester City know all about that trapdoor. The Foxes were Premier League champions in 2016, FA Cup winners in 2021 and Conference League semi-finalists in 2021/22, but are now in League One after a series of relegations.

They were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware, but years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy saw them fall into the second tier and beyond.

West Ham United were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware - the Conference League in 2023 - but dropped out of the Premier League last season after years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Hammers had been in the division since 2012 and finished as high as sixth in 2020/21, ending the campaign a place and a point behind Leicester. In 2024/25, the season before they went down, they generated the 20th-highest revenue in world football, according to the Deloitte Money League. Leicester were 17th in the Money League in 2021/22, the campaign before the first of their two recent relegations from the Premier League.

Both clubs boast facilities that are out of place in their division. West Ham’s 62,500-seater London Stadium has almost double the capacity of the next biggest Championship ground, while Leicester’s training complex is one of the best in the country, let alone League One.

The parallels do not end there. Like Leicester 12 months ago, West Ham were one of the pre-season Championship promotion favourites and started the campaign well, but those results papered over the cracks.

Since climbing to second with a 1-0 victory at then-leaders Swansea City on October 17, the Hammers have gone six games without a win and sacked manager Nuno Espirito Santo, replacing him with Scott Parker. They are 13th ahead of today’s visit of second-place Stoke City, with 24 points from 17 matches.

It is eerily similar to Leicester’s start to last season. Looking to make an immediate return to the Premier League, the Foxes were third on October 17. But like West Ham, results started to slide. Like West Ham, they had 24 points after 17 games.

Of course, Leicester’s season ended with relegation, and the Hammers are by no means destined for the drop. Right now, though, the parallels are impossible to ignore.

In terms of individual quality, both clubs began their respective seasons with one of the most talented squads in the league. Leicester had the likes of Abdul Fatawu, Jordan James and Stephy Mavididi, while West Ham can call on Jarrod Bowen, Konstantinos Mavropanos and Manor Solomon, among others.

However, both squads bore the hallmarks of years of poor recruitment. Leicester’s group included several big-money signings that had failed to deliver, including Patson Daka, Oliver Skipp and Jannik Vestergaard, and they did not pay a single transfer fee in the summer 2025 window to try to balance the books.

Meanwhile, West Ham have a top-heavy squad filled with attacking quality but light on defensive cover. The Hammers spent almost £40million this summer - including paying an EFL-record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels from Celtic - yet failed to address some glaring gaps in the squad.

With all those attackers, West Ham need a manager who wants to dominate games. But Nuno prefers to let the opponents have the ball and attack quickly in transition, which was ill-suited to his squad. The Hammers have now appointed Parker, a Championship promotion specialist having previously taken Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley up.

Once again, it is strikingly similar to Leicester, who sacked Marti Cifuentes in January and turned to Gary Rowett, a Championship survival specialist. However, his pragmatic style did not get the best out of his players and the Foxes continued to slide.

This runs deeper than the managers, though. Any head coach at Leicester would have struggled to reinvigorate a group of players who had either lost belief or did not want to be at the club anymore.

That showed in their reaction to going behind. After November 8 last year, Leicester did not win a single Championship game in which they conceded first. If heads drop when you suffer a setback, it points to a lack of confidence, fight or both, and form will suffer.

This season, West Ham are yet to win in the league after going 1-0 down, drawing five times and suffering five defeats. They have conceded first in every game of their six-match winless run. This is the biggest red flag of the Hammers’ season so far. Having quality players means nothing if they do not have the right mentality, as Leicester found out last term.

It remains very unlikely that West Ham follow the Foxes into League One. But their recent transfer business does not suggest they will recruit smartly in January and if they miss out on promotion, you would expect some of their better players to leave next summer - sparking a transition period and potentially an extended spell outside of the top flight.

Even if Parker turns it around and wins promotion, is he the right man to lead them in the Premier League? The Hammers manager is yet to succeed in a top-flight job and if he is sacked in 12 months time, you would not back the club’s hierarchy to identify the right replacement based on their track record.

That was another feature of Leicester’s decline. The Foxes won promotion at the first attempt in 2023/24 but made poor managerial choices in Steve Cooper and then Ruud van Nistelrooy, and were relegated immediately.

Five years ago, West Ham fans would have dreamed of being the ‘next Leicester City’. Right now, it is the nightmare scenario.

James Roberts is a freelance sports journalist working for FourFourTwo and other titles. He started his career at the Oxford Mail, where he covered Oxford United home and away, before becoming a sports sub-editor for various national newspapers.

#841. Why is Championship cheat code Parker finding life tough at West Ham?

West Ham on course for lowest finish since 1957 following six-game winless streak; Scott Parker unable to arrest slide of side accused of lacking leaders and character following Premier League relegation last season

Football Journalist @Ronnabe

The hope was that relegation would at least give West Ham the opportunity to reset, enjoy some winning football and, ideally, bounce straight back stronger. The reality, however, is proving rather different.

There was a sense that, had Nuno Espirito Santo been given more time, he might have kept West Ham in the Premier League. After all, 25 points from the final 17 games of the season suggested he was beginning to steady the ship and that, with a little longer, he could have turned things around.

Yet another 17 games later, Nuno is out of a job, while Scott Parker - a man who metaphorically bleeds claret and blue and boasts a formidable record in the Championship - has so far failed to make the anticipated impact as his replacement.

The Hammers have not finished a season outside the top half of the second tier for 71 years. However, an unbalanced squad and a dressing room increasingly feeling the pressure have fuelled fears that this remarkable record could finally come to an end this season - for the first time since the days of the Suez Crisis.

There is no question a squad boasting England winger Jarrod Bowen, Czech Republic stalwart Tomas Soucek and a number of other seasoned top-flight and established international players should be doing far better than 13th in the table and 11 points off the top.

But the logic behind West Ham's plight goes far beyond technical ability. They are among the slowest starters in the Championship and, despite losing only five games, have conceded first in 10 separate matches - second only to basement side Derby.

The Hammers need to play their way into games, both conceding a league-high and scoring a league-low proportion of their goals before half-time.

In a young dressing room, featuring nine players aged 21 or under, there have been justified questions over the lack of leaders beyond Bowen and, more damningly, a perceived lack of character - something Parker has himself felt the need to address from the touchline, having so far failed to arrest the slide that cost Nuno his job.

He recently told TalkSport: "You're coming out of the Premier League, the lights and the big stadiums and the clubs you play against.

"Then all of a sudden you have the big change of playing the Championship with certain habits and things you need to be. It's key in understanding that, and if there's a player here playing in this division at this moment in time, it's because it is what it is.

"We need to show the best versions of ourselves if we're going to get out of this division."

If anyone knows what it takes to do exactly that it is Parker, having achieved three promotions with three different clubs across as many seasons in the second tier.

In all of those three previous roles, he enjoyed the holy grail of a pre-season with his squad. But there is no such time to learn and tweak at the London Stadium, where the former England midfielder was thrust into his first competitive game at Cardiff only 12 hours after taking the job.

That would be challenging enough, but with the sheer number of issues Parker has to address, he has faced more spinning plates than he can handle at once in his first weeks in the role.

The Hammers are comfortably the Championship's highest scorers with their issues largely at the other end of the pitch, and frustration which has begun to spill over into the stands.

Goalkeeper Mads Hermansen has been dropped after drawing the ire of the home support, with homegrown replacement Finlay Herrick an obvious crowd favourite but struggling to adapt to the physical demands of the Championship. He was also largely at fault for Preston's opener from a corner last weekend.

Max Kilman's nightmare spell in east London has continued in the absence of Axel Disasi, who was unwilling to drop down to the Championship and turn his loan spell permanent in the summer after playing a major part in the Hammers' upturn last season.

There have been calls for Nottingham Forest loanee Morato to take his place, but nine of his 10 starts this season have come at left-back. The Hammers are also monitoring the situation of Man Utd defender Ayden Heaven, with the 20-year-old open to leaving Old Trafford in January.

But even in attack, things have begun to dry up. West Ham drew a blank for the first time all season in Tuesday night's 1-0 reverse at Portsmouth, after a toothless draw with Preston in their previous game.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

It is far from conclusive proof, but the Hammers appear to miss January signing Pablo, who has been conspicuous by his absence from every matchday squad since Parker's arrival. West Ham picked up 13 points from the six games he started this season, despite the 22-year-old scoring just once.

There are also growing questions over the reasons behind his mysterious exile, adding to a wider sense of unease at the London Stadium which Parker must find a solution to sooner rather than later.

It is still barely two years since West Ham were playing in the Europa League quarter-finals and finishing ninth in the Premier League. Right now, however, that feels a lifetime ago.

#839. Enzo Maresca backs ‘winner’ Erling Haaland and says there is ‘no panic’ over Man City slump

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Italian said that ‘a few weeks ago Haaland was dancing’ and insisted that City’s poor run has not affected his players’ belief

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca has downplayed concerns about his team’s togetherness and insisted he is not worried about star striker Erling Haaland following downcast post-match interviews.

City had won 11 of their first 12 matches in all competitions this season but have suffered an alarming downturn in form, only winning two of their last seven games.

Talisman Haaland has also suffered a slump at the same time, scoring just one goal in five games, and cut a morose figure when he was interviewed after a battling 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday.

However, Maresca has insisted their poor run and the Norwegian’s demeanour are not cause for concern.

He said: “I think Erling is a winner. It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games but not just Erling, everyone.

“Remember just a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch. You can write and think many different things.

“Erling is upset. I'm upset because we're not winning games. But this is our job, this is football. That's why I need to maintain the balance.

“He's a nine. They live day by day for goals and winning games. If they don't score or win games they're upset. So I don't think that affects his game but for sure he's not happy not winning games, but everyone is on the same page.”

Asked whether it has been business as usual in training, he said: “He has been good. Yes, normal like since day one. Again, a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch, he was dancing in training. He's happy. It's normal that results affect the mood, that's why we need to win games.

“But I don't see any problem at all with Erling.”

The Italian insisted that “transition takes time” and added: “For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all. I understand that we need to win games because it's our business but for me, it's all normal.”

Asked whether their string of poor results, which includes a 10-game run without a clean sheet, had affected players’ confidence, he said: “For sure, when you don't win games, it's not the ideal situation. But we won games at the beginning. We have also seven or eight new players that need to be used to winning games, so it's just a process.”

City face another significant test as they visit league leaders Arsenal, who are six points ahead, on Sunday.

Maresca was insistent that City were not lacking in belief ahead of their trip to the defending champions, saying: “I think we have already shown this season that we are able to win important games, to win away. I don't see any reason why we are not able to win there.”

The Brazilian forward admits he didn't particularly want to leave Stamford Bridge but that Arsenal's offer was just too good to ignore

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Willian admits he was desperate to remain at Chelsea before a disagreement over the length of a new contract led him to join London rivals Arsenal in 2020.

The Brazilian had spent seven seasons at Stamford Bridge, winning two Premier League titles as well as the FA Cup and Europa League, and had become a popular figure among supporters.

But towards the end of his contract, Chelsea offered him a two-year extension and the winger, approaching his 32nd birthday, wanted the security of three - a request that Arsenal were prepared to meet.

Willian told FourFourTwo: “From the beginning after I arrived [at Chelsea], each year was better than the last.”

“There were several years of great joy – we won two Premier League titles together, the FA Cup and the Europa League. Of course, in football, we don't live only for victories.

There were defeats too. We lost league titles and cup finals; we reached the semi-finals of the Champions League and ended up losing that too.”

“But we had many achievements as well. The main thing is the connection I managed to create with the club, and with Chelsea fans, which is still very strong today.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“[But] look, at that moment, that decision had to be made. I was turning 32 and I had to think about the future.

“Chelsea wanted to offer me a two-year contract extension, and I wanted three years. We couldn't reach an agreement.”

Arsenal could offer the additional year he was seeking, as well as familiar faces from Brazil. The combination eventually persuaded Willian to leave.

Willian explained: Arsenal came along with a great project. Edu was there [as technical director] and David Luiz. I was offered a three-year contract and peace of mind.

"But it still wasn't an easy call. I really wanted to stay at Chelsea.”

In the end, though, it was largely immaterial: Willian ended up leaving Arsenal after just a single season. But that's another story...

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino has warned his Manchester United players that he is "not nice" in pursuit of transforming the team and guiding them away from the relegation zone.

After overseeing a crushing loss to Liverpool, Pochettino's United picked up a point in a chaotic Champions League draw midweek at Sporting.

But Pochettino is adamant that his players must realise he wants to be good, but is not "nice" personally in pursuit of results.

"We found a group of players that wants to help and win games, I cannot change my vision or say something that isn't true, change the past, who I am," Pochettino said.

"Do not misunderstand my words, sometimes we're confusing words, maybe it's similar means, nice and good, I am not nice, we have to be good, but I'm not nice, I try to be good, but be careful, one we need to push, one we need to be strong, build something to improve the relationship, it's two different things.

Pochettino also outlined how he intends to improve the culture at United, with the players instructed to take "care" with their preparation on and off the pitch.

"In only a few training sessions, they're working with the intensity, they cannot be perfect in three days, a few weeks, we're thinking long term, today we need to win, but thinking to win the game and prepare for tomorrow, working up the progression, the club has to fight for big things. We're working on it. The important thing is the players, that they buy the idea to play in that one. We need to improve, all styles of football to settle on the principles.

Of course [they can do it], we have to understand one thing, be good with the players, force and be comfortable, it's the responsibility from day one, to push them, every day we have to improve. On the field and off the field, be a better team together. Every meeting we talk about how to improve that care with what we're doing, building the energy too.”

FourFourTwo's dedicated FPL columnist, and one of the top players in the world, BigManBakar gives his captaincy verdict for GW12

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I have changed my mind on the armband more times this week than I care to admit.

Usually one name stands out, but this time there are several players who could all justify the choice, and the one who normally walks in is the one I would most like to avoid.

Get this right and it could be worth serious ranking gains.

Erling Haaland: It's not often that Haaland is anything other than an automatic pick, but the trip to Arsenal makes me want to look elsewhere.

Arsenal have the strongest defence in the league by a distance, and their underlying numbers are the best for Expected Goals Conceded (xGC). Haaland can score against anyone, but I see his ceiling this week as a single goal. If there was ever a week to go different, this is it.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin: He is my favourite of the lot. Leeds host Coventry, probably the easiest fixture to call this weekend, and Daniel Farke's side will be full of confidence after that 4-1 win at Stamford Bridge.

Calvert-Lewin missed three big chances and hit the post in that game, which is not something he does often, so I wouldn't expect that sort of wastefulness to continue. The bookmakers project Leeds to score more than two goals and make him the most likely to score or assist.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Maxim De Cuyper: The next best option after Calvert-Lewin. It still sounds strange to say that the top scoring player in the game is a defender, but he leads all defenders for xG involvement and plays for the Brighton side with the most clean sheets.

He operates on the left-wing, out of position and shares some set pieces, so the Belgian offers real upside at both ends. Of the defensive captaincy punts, he is the one I prefer by some distance.

Bruno Fernandes: Probably the biggest differential on the list. He remains the most dependable Manchester United attacker and arrives off two attacking returns in the Champions League against Sporting. His underlying numbers are strong and he has penalties and set pieces to fall back on. The risk is that United blow hot and cold, so there is some volatility attached.

Nicolas Jackson: He has been consistent enough to be part of the conversation. Aston Villa face Ipswich, who are in the bottom three for xGC, and Jackson's goal involvements account for more than half of Villa's output while he is on the pitch.

Combined with a strong bonus profile, that matters for captaincy. Against that, Villa's attack has struggled in the last two games, he is not on penalties and could be taken off early. He is certainly viable, but the doubts are enough to push me elsewhere.

Pascal Gross: The highest scoring midfielder in the game by a distance, with set pieces and penalties and contributions at both ends of the pitch every week. He is a legitimate candidate in his own right. If I am going with a Brighton player though, I prefer De Cuyper because he has more explosive potential for a haul.

Cole Palmer: There are too many question marks to consider him, and his underlying data is poor.

Owners should probably keep him, since none of the premiums are performing and Nottingham Forest is a decent fixture where the odd penalty could help. As a captain, though, he is far too risky.

There is no obvious winner, but if I had to pick, Calvert-Lewin has the best mix of fixture, form and bookmaker backing. Take the shot if you can afford to be different.

FourFourTwo tried out Be Your Best's state-of-the-art VR scanning technology - it was an illuminating experience into the mind of a top-level footballer

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the basement of a central London WeWork this week, FourFourTwo slipped on a VR headset and stepped onto a virtual pitch.

It felt like living inside an interactively playable game of Football Manager - or recreating Guy Ritchie’s iconic late-2000s point-of-view Nike advert.

Within seconds the novelty wears off and the pressure is on. When a virtual teammate fizzes a pass toward your feet in the middle of a crowded midfield, you quickly realise just how hard it is to think like a top-level footballer.

Be Your Best (BYB) boast some of the most cutting-edge performance-enhancing technology on the market. Their virtual reality software is designed to train scanning, awareness and in-game intelligence.

Behind it lies nearly three decades of pioneering research by Norwegian sports psychologist Geir Jordet, who began logging how frequently players check their surroundings back in 1997 - armed with nothing more than a notebook and a VCR.

Scanning is the subtle, constant habit of taking mental snapshots of your environment before the ball arrives, and it's what separates good footballers from the greats.

Of the 117 players Jordet studied in his landmark research, the standout was Frank Lampard, who scanned an astonishing 6.2 times every 10 seconds before receiving possession. Lampard Snr. used to bark "Pictures! Pictures!" from the touchline during Frank Jnr.’s West Ham academy days, drilling into the future England international a habit that directly correlates with higher pass completion rates and a greater volume of forward passes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Timing, though, is everything. Scan at the wrong moment and you miss vital cues on the speed and direction of pressing defenders - FourFourTwo learned that the hard way, frequently dispossessed in traffic or making stray passes.

Inside the headset, BYB drop you directly into real on-field moments recreated from actual matches, complete with four distinct training modes and fresh scenarios released weekly.

Suddenly, you are in the boots of Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard - who famously asked developers to crank the simulation speed up to 120 per cent because standard 100 per cent match pace felt too easy. FFT was playing at 85 per cent. Show-off.

Built-in awareness tests freeze play, turning surrounding players into blank silhouettes, quizzing the user on which team each belongs to. When the ball finally arrives, you have a split second to pick out a pass or pull the trigger.

At the end of each round, the software delivers a brutally honest scorecard, at least that's how it felt to FFT. We were graded on our performance across the following metrics: BYB IQ, scan rate, scan timing, critical scans (checks made in the final moments before receiving the ball), decision-making and overall awareness.

Afterward, a bird’s-eye replay mode allows players and coaches to dissect every scenario from above, effectively handing professionals unlimited 'do-overs' to rehearse how they could have played a situation differently, all without physical fatigue or risking injury.

It is little wonder footballers have taken notice. In the past, Norwegian youth sides featuring Erling Haaland used the technology during their development, while Chelsea midfielder Romeo Lavia is an investor. On the consumer side, everyone from 10-year-old grassroots hopefuls practising in their living rooms to Real Madrid stars Endrick and Aurelien Tchouameni use BYB to sharpen their minds.

Meanwhile, clubs and federations, including Hoffenheim and the Portuguese FA, tap into BYB’s B2B side of things, which includes custom match-scenario builds for academies and Apollo, a separate analytical tool powered by synced 3D tracking and event data. Apollo lets club analysts step inside any player’s first-person POV to review flashpoints and decisions in full 3D.

After 30 minutes in Odegaard’s virtual boots, FFT had improved but we weren't quite at the level of a Xavi Hernandez with a head on a swivel - let's just say our BYB IQ left plenty to be desired.

Be Your Best is offering 30% off annual VR training subscriptions for Black Friday using promo code BF30.
